1. Executive Summary 
Scribl set out to test a single question: can generative AI assemble the drawings from a game 
session into a single, shareable keepsake -- without redrawing or "interpreting" anyone's art? 

  info@missioncloud.com 
 2026 Mission Cloud Services, Inc. Proprietary & Confidential.  2 
Earlier experiments had taken too much creative liberty, turning a participant's stick-figure dog 
into something that was no longer theirs. 
Over a three-week, time-boxed engagement, Mission built a working pipeline that proves the 
concept. It takes the raw drawings and prompt from a Scribl session and produces a composed 
scene image where every participant's original artwork is preserved pixel-for-pixel -- never 
regenerated. Generative AI is used only for the connective tissue around the art: understanding 
what each drawing depicts, generating a hand-drawn-style background that matches the 
session, and intelligently arranging the cards into a coherent scene. 
The result: the original art stays true (the North Star from discovery), the output looks 
composed rather than like "alphabet soup," and the whole thing runs automatically -- removing 
the manual drag-and-resize work that hosts do today. 
This is a proof of concept, delivered as a documented, runnable Python pipeline on AWS 
Bedrock. It validates feasibility and gives Scribl a concrete foundation -- and a clear set of knobs 
 -- to decide whether and how to productize.

Key design choice: the participants' drawings are only ever masked and placed -- never sent to 
an image model for regeneration. Fidelity to the original art is structurally guaranteed, not just 
prompted for. 
Per-step model selection: Each AI stage can be pointed at a different model via `config.json`. For 
example, the Describe stage (Stage 2) now uses Claude Sonnet 4.6 instead of Opus 4.8 -- 
improving performance and reducing cost while preserving quality -- while higher-judgment 
stages can remain on Opus.

5. Time & Cost Factors 
Every run writes a `pipeline_report.md` breaking down duration and Bedrock token usage per 
stage, priced from the rates in `config.json`. The figures below are planning-level estimates. 
What drives cost and time (per session): 
Factor Impact 
Number of drawings Largest driver. Stage 2 (Describe) makes one 
Claude call per drawing; more cards = more calls 
and a longer composition plan. Parallel 
description calls now keep wall-clock time low 
even for large sessions. 
Refinement iterations (`--refine-iterations`, 
default 3) 
Each iteration is a multi-image Claude call. Stops 
early when Claude is satisfied, so cost is often 
below the cap. 
Model choice Opus gives the best planning quality; a 
smaller/faster Claude model (e.g. Sonnet 4.6) 
materially cuts cost where quality allows. Models 
are now selectable per stage (see Tuning). 
Background generation One Claude prompt call + one Stability render per 
session -- roughly fixed per artifact. 
Masking & composition Effectively free -- local CPU image processing, no 
model calls. 
 
Where the model spend concentrates: the AI cost is dominated by the image-heavy stages -- 
Describe (one image per card) and Refine (two images per iteration). Output tokens are small; 
input/image tokens dominate. The two non-AI stages (Mask, Compose) add only local compute 
time. 
Cost-control levers already built in: 
- `--refine-iterations` caps the most expensive stage; early-stop avoids wasted calls. 
- `--skip-*` flags let you re-run only changed stages instead of paying for the whole pipeline. 
- Stage 2 describe-calls run concurrently, shortening wall-clock time (~7 min -> under 2 min 
on large sessions). 
- Per-step model selection lets you route cheaper stages to lower-cost models (e.g. Sonnet 
4.6 for Describe). 
- Per-stage reporting makes it trivial to spot the costliest step before scaling up.

6. Pricing & Cost Reporting 
The pipeline emits accurate, per-stage cost reporting on every run. `config.json` supports 
model-specific pricing, so each model's input and output token rates are tracked independently 
 -- meaning reports remain correct even when different stages use different models. As Bedrock 
rates change, you update them in one place (`config.json -> pricing`) and all reports stay 
accurate. 
Example pricing configured in `config.json`: 
Model Input rate Output rate 
Claude Opus 4.8 $15.00 / 1M tokens $25.00 / 1M tokens 
Claude Sonnet 4.6 $3.00 / 1M tokens $15.00 / 1M tokens 
 
Because pricing is tracked per model, a report can blend Opus (planning/refinement) and 
Sonnet (description) costs and still produce an accurate total.

8. Areas for Improvement & Future Enhancements 
The POC proves feasibility; the following would raise quality and unlock the broader vision 
discussed in discovery. 
Quality & fidelity 
- Multi-scene backgrounds. Today the AI generates a single background scene per artifact 
(e.g. a kitchen or a park) -- you get one scene or the other. A future enhancement would 
test prompts that generate multiple scenes in one image (e.g. a kitchen and a park 
together), so drawings that belong indoors are placed inside and outdoor drawings are 
placed outside. This needs further prompt testing. 
- AI grouping of drawings. Add a dedicated AI round that groups related drawings together 
before placement, then positions each group meaningfully. This would be especially 
valuable for larger sessions with many participants, producing more coherent, story-like 
compositions. 
- Dedicated per-artifact backgrounds for large groups. When a large session splits into 
multiple artifacts, the same background is currently reused across all of them. Giving each 
artifact its own dedicated, distinct background would make multi-artifact outputs feel like 
different scenes. This ties naturally into the AI grouping feature above -- related drawings 
could be paired together and placed on a background dedicated to that group. 
- User-provided drawing labels. Letting a participant add a one-line caption ("my dog from 
when I was five") would beat AI-inferred descriptions on accuracy and cut Stage 2 cost -- 
exactly the trade-off raised in discovery. 
- Transcript / sentiment integration. Once Scribl captures session audio (e.g., via the planned 
Zoom integration), real transcripts could drive richer, more personal compositions. 

  info@missioncloud.com 
 2026 Mission Cloud Services, Inc. Proprietary & Confidential.  9 
- Smarter placement & "integration." Today cards are arranged logically; the discovery vision 
of true integration (the family walking with the ice cream under the palm tree) is a natural 
next target. 
- Stroke-level data. Scribl's Metabase stores every stroke as vector data. This opens the door 
to animation, live "drawing playback," and joint-aware posing -- a distinctive, hard-to-copy 
feature. 
- Scribl Provided Templates. Have templatized scribble artifacts provided by Scribl designers 
to influence background generation. This could assist with consistent branding/themes.  
Robustness & operations 
- Style consistency across backgrounds (seed/style controls) so a brand or campaign feels 
cohesive. 
- Multi-round handling -- currently focused on single-round per the agreed POC scope; 
combining rounds is a known extension. 
- Evaluation harness -- formalize the "what makes a good artifact" criteria into a repeatable 
scoring pass for regression-testing prompt changes. 
9. Recommended Next Phase 
The POC ran as a local, script-based pipeline by design -- the right scope to prove the concept. 
The natural next step is to operationalize it as a live service inside Scribl's product, along the 
architecture envisioned in the SOW. 
Phase 2 -- Productionize & Integrate (recommended): 
1. Deploy as an API. Wrap the pipeline behind API Gateway + AWS Lambda in Scribl's AWS 
account (per the SOW architecture): client uploads assets to S3, invokes the API, and 
receives the finished artifact. Secure with an API key for the POC-to-pilot stage. 
2. Live integration. Hook the API into the end-of-session flow so artifacts generate 
automatically -- eliminating manual host effort entirely. 
3. Add the highest-value input: user captions. Ship the optional one-line drawing label; it's the 
cheapest, highest-impact quality lever identified. 
4. Pilot & measure. Run real sessions through the deployed service, using the built-in 
cost/time reporting to validate per-artifact economics at scale before committing to 
features. 
5. Then expand selectively based on pilot results -- transcript integration, true compositional 
"integration," AI grouping with dedicated multi-scene backgrounds, and the stroke-data 
animation track as a differentiated bet. 
Suggested sequence: Deploy -> Integrate -> add captions -> Pilot & measure -> expand. This 
keeps each step funded by demonstrated value and aligned to Scribl's budget sensitivity.

10. Appendix -- Running the Pipeline 
Full setup and options are in `README.md`. Quick reference: 
```bash 
One session, end-to-end 
python masking/run_pipeline.py \ 
  --session "files/Single Round Games/<uuid> - <prompt>" 
With drop shadows and 3 refinement passes 
python masking/run_pipeline.py \ 
  --session "files/Single Round Games/<uuid> - <prompt>" \ 
  --shadow --refine-iterations 3 
All sessions, consolidated batch report 
python masking/run_all_sessions.py 
``` 
Outputs land under `masking/output/<session>/`: 
- `compose_output/composite_canvas.png` -- the final artifact 
- `pipeline_report.md` -- per-stage timing and cost 
- `descriptions.json`, `composition_plan.json`, `background.png` -- intermediate artifacts for 
inspection 
Prerequisites: Python 3.11+, AWS Bedrock access in `us-east-1`, and model access enabled for 
the configured Claude and Stability AI models.
